title: Beatrix and the Orbit
premise: Jude Joubert, the last navigator aboard the colony ship Beatrix, has spent eleven years tending a navigation beacon that no one in the settlement remembers ordering — and guarding the hold where the ship's original crew sleeps as digital backups. When the colony's children begin dreaming identical dreams of a burning village on the planet below, Jude realizes the beacon is broadcasting those dreams, and that the 'empty' world they colonized was not empty at all. As the corporate charter's records insist no massacre ever occurred and the jump window home closes in nineteen days, Jude must choose between protecting the sleeping backups — the last remnant of the crew who raised her — and exposing them as the architects of the cover-up. In the end, Jude wakes one backup, her mentor Captain Osei, who confesses and chooses to testify, letting the truth broadcast to Earth even as the Beatrix burns up in the jump; the children's dream finally goes quiet, and the colonists stay, becoming inheritors rather than conquerors.
about_author: Paloma Winterbourne is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent six years maintaining lighthouses off the Hebridean coast before turning to science fiction. Her work explores inherited guilt and the machinery of memory, and she writes all first drafts by hand in tide tables' margins.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She makes her weekly climb to the beacon tower above the colony, checking a transmitter whose maintenance logs predate the landing itself. The emotional beat is quiet loneliness: Jude talks to the machine because no one else remembers why it exists, establishing her isolation and her strange inheritance from the dead-seeming crew.

chapters.title: Children of the Same Dream
chapters.summary: Alternating between Jude and nine-year-old Sefu Okonkwo. Sefu wakes screaming from a dream of fire and a river of ash; so did every child in the settlement. Jude recognizes the dream's geography — it matches coordinates in the beacon's restricted memory banks. The beat is dread disguised as coincidence.

chapters.title: What Sleeps in the Hold
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She descends into the sealed hold and confronts the backups: two hundred sleeping minds of the original crew, including Captain Osei, who trained her. She finds an encrypted directive addressed to herself, unopenable until the jump window opens. The beat is betrayal anticipated — love curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Charter Says Otherwise
chapters.summary: Sefu's POV. The children are pulled into the dream together, waking with shared knowledge of a village called Meridian and names none of them have heard. Meanwhile the colonial administrator, Voss, publicly dismisses the dreams as fever, citing the charter's pristine survey records. The beat is gaslighting at community scale.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She decodes part of the directive: the beacon isn't transmitting dreams — it's receiving them, from something alive beneath the ash plain. The jump window countdown begins, and Voss orders the beacon shut down. Jude must sabotage her own post to keep it running. The beat is open rebellion.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: Sefu leads Jude through the dream-walk to the physical ruins of Meridian, where they find fused foundations, child-sized bones, and a surviving native intelligence buried in the geology — the dreamer itself. It shows Jude the massacre through borrowed eyes. The beat is witness: horror transformed into obligation.

chapters.title: Every Record Lies
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She confronts Voss with physical evidence; he reveals the charter's records were rewritten before landing, and that the backups voted unanimously for the purge. The colonists' entire legitimacy rests on the lie. The beat is vertigo — everything Jude belongs to is built on erasure.

chapters.title: The Vote in the Dark
chapters.summary: Sefu's POV. The children, still dreaming, begin refusing to wake — anchoring themselves in the dreamer's memory as protest. The colony fractures: some parents side with Voss, others follow the children's evidence. Jude realizes waking Osei is her only path to testimony. The beat is desperate resolve.

chapters.title: Osei Wakes
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, climax. Against protocol and her own fear, Jude wakes Captain Osei, who confesses to the massacre and chooses to stand before the colony and the buried dreamer alike. Voss attempts to force the early jump; the beacon, guided by the children, holds the ship down. The beat is reckoning — loyalty fulfilled through truth.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Shared POV, resolution. The Beatrix jumps empty, carrying only Osei's recorded confession toward Earth as the window closes behind it. The colonists hold a mourning for Meridian, the children's dream fades to silence, and the dreamer offers the settlement a covenant instead of vengeance. Jude tends the beacon still — now a memorial, not a secret. The beat is grief transmuted into belonging.
